'''Trophic coherence''' is a property of [[directed graph]]s (or directed [[Complex networks|networks]]).<ref name="johnson2014">{{cite journal |author=Johnson S, Domı́nguez-Garcı́a V, Donetti L, Muñoz MA |year=2014 |title=Trophic coherence determines food-web stability |journal=[[Proc Natl Acad Sci USA]] |volume=111 |issue=50 |pages=17923–17928 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1409077111 |pmid=25468963 |pmc=4273378 |arxiv=1404.7728 |bibcode=2014PNAS..11117923J |doi-access=free }}</ref> It is based on the concept of [[trophic levels]] used mainly in [[ecology]],<ref>{{cite journal |author=Levine S |year=1980 |title=Several measures of trophic structure applicable to complex food webs |journal=[[J Theor Biol]] |volume=83 |issue=2 |pages=195–207|doi=10.1016/0022-5193(80)90288-X |bibcode=1980JThBi..83..195L }}</ref> but which can be defined for directed networks in general and provides a measure of hierarchical structure among nodes. Trophic coherence is the tendency of nodes to fall into well-defined trophic levels. It has been related to several structural and dynamical properties of directed networks, including the prevalence of [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycles]]<ref name="johnson2017">{{cite journal |author=Johnson S and Jones NS |year=2017 |title=Looplessness in networks is linked to trophic coherence |journal=[[Proc Natl Acad Sci USA]] |volume=114 |issue=22 |pages=5618–5623 | doi=10.1073/pnas.1613786114 |pmid=28512222 |pmc=5465891 | arxiv=1505.07332|doi-access=free |bibcode=2017PNAS..114.5618J }}</ref> and [[network motif]]s,<ref name="klaise2017">{{cite journal |author=Klaise J and Johnson S |title=The origin of motif families in food webs | year=2017 | journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |volume=7|issue=1 | pages=16197| doi=10.1038/s41598-017-15496-1 | doi-access=free|pmid=29170384 |pmc=5700930 |arxiv=1609.04318|bibcode=2017NatSR...716197K}}</ref> [[ecological stability]],<ref name="johnson2014"/> intervality,<ref name="dominguez2016">{{cite journal |author=Domı́nguez-Garcı́a V, Johnson S, Muñoz MA |year=2016 |title=Intervality and coherence in complex networks |journal=[[Chaos (journal)|Chaos]] |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=065308 |doi=10.1063/1.4953163 |pmid=27368797 |arxiv=1603.03767 |bibcode=2016Chaos..26f5308D |s2cid=16081869 }}</ref> and spreading processes like [[Mathematical modelling of infectious disease|epidemics]] and [[Critical brain hypothesis|neuronal avalanches]].<ref name="klaise2016">{{cite journal |author=Klaise J and Johnson S |year=2016 |title=From neurons to epidemics: How trophic coherence affects spreading processes |journal=[[Chaos (journal)|Chaos]] |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=065310 |doi=10.1063/1.4953160 |pmid=27368799 |arxiv=1603.00670 |bibcode=2016Chaos..26f5310K |s2cid=205214650 }}</ref>

== Definition ==

[[File:Networks with different trophic coherence.png|600px|thumb|Two directed networks generated with the 'generalised preferential preying model'. The position of the nodes on the vertical axis represents their trophic level. The network on the left is maximally coherent (q=0), while the one on the right is more incoherent (q=0.49).]]

Consider a directed network defined by  
the <math>N\times N</math> [[adjacency matrix]] <math>A=(a_{ij})</math>.
Each node <math>i</math> can be assigned a [[trophic level]] <math>s_i</math> according to
::<math>
s_i=1+\frac{1}{k_i^\text{in}}\sum_j a_{ij} s_j,
</math>
where <math>k_i^\text{in}=\sum_j a_{ij}</math> is <math>i</math>'s in-degree, and nodes 
with <math>k_i^\text{in}=0</math> (basal nodes) have <math>s_i=1</math> by convention.
Each edge has a ''trophic difference'' associated, defined as <math>x_{ij}=s_i-s_j</math>.
The ''trophic coherence'' of the network is a measure of how tightly peaked the distribution of trophic distances,
<math>p(x)</math>, 
is around its mean value, which is always <math>\langle x\rangle =1</math>.
This can be captured by an ''incoherence parameter'' <math>q</math>, 
equal to the [[standard deviation]] of <math>p(x)</math>:
::<math>
q=\sqrt{\frac{1}{L}\sum_{ij}a_{ij}x_{ij}^2 -1},
</math>
where <math>L=\sum_{ij}a_{ij}</math> is the number of edges in the network.<ref name="johnson2014"/>

The figure shows two networks which differ in their trophic coherence. The position of the nodes on the vertical axis corresponds to their trophic level. In the network on the left, nodes fall into distinct (integer) trophic levels, so the network is maximally coherent <math>(q=0)</math>. 
In the one on the right, many of the nodes have fractional trophic levels, and the network is more incoherent <math>(q=0.49)</math>.<ref name="klaise2016"/>

== Trophic coherence in nature ==

The degree to which empirical networks are trophically coherent (or incoherent) can be investigated by comparison with a [[null model]].
This is provided by the ''basal ensemble'', which comprises networks in which all non-basal nodes have the same proportion of basal nodes
for in-neighbours.<ref name="johnson2017"/> Expected values in this ensemble converge to those of the widely used ''configuration ensemble''<ref name="newman2003">{{cite journal|author=Newman, MEJ  |year=2003 |title=The structure and function of complex networks |journal=[[SIAM Review]] |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=167–256 |doi=10.1137/S003614450342480 |arxiv=cond-mat/0303516 |bibcode=2003SIAMR..45..167N |s2cid=221278130 }}</ref> in the limit <math>N\rightarrow\infty</math>, <math>L/N\rightarrow\infty</math> (with <math>N</math> and <math>L</math> the numbers of nodes and edges), 
and can be shown numerically to be a good approximation for finite random networks. The basal ensemble expectation for the incoherence parameter is
::<math>
\tilde{q}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{L_B}-1},
</math>
where <math>L_B</math> is the number of edges connected to basal nodes.<ref name="johnson2017"/>
The ratio <math>q/\tilde{q}</math> measured in empirical networks reveals whether they are more or less coherent than the random expectation.
For instance, Johnson and Jones<ref name="johnson2017"/> find in a set of networks that [[food webs]] are significantly coherent <math>(q/\tilde{q}=0.44 \pm 0.17)</math>, [[metabolic networks]] are significantly incoherent <math>(q/\tilde{q}=1.81 \pm 0.11)</math>, and [[gene regulatory networks]] are close to the random expectation <math>(q/\tilde{q}=0.99 \pm 0.05)</math>.

== Trophic levels and node function ==

There is as yet little understanding of the mechanisms which might lead to particular kinds of networks becoming significantly 
coherent or incoherent.<ref name="johnson2017"/> However, in systems which present correlations between trophic level and other features of nodes,
processes which tended to favour the creation of edges between nodes with particular characteristics could induce coherence or incoherence.
In the case of food webs, predators tend to specialise on consuming prey with certain biological properties (such as size, speed or behaviour) 
which correlate with their diet, and hence with trophic level. 
This has been suggested as the reason for food-web coherence.<ref name="johnson2014"/> However, food-web models based on a ''niche axis'' do not reproduce realistic trophic coherence,<ref name="johnson2014"/> which may mean either that this explanation is insufficient, or that several [[ecological niche|niche dimensions]] need to be considered.<ref name="rossberg2010">{{cite journal |author=Rossberg AG, Brännström A, Dieckmann U |year=2010 |title=Food-web structure in low- and high-dimensional trophic niche spaces |journal=[[Journal of the Royal Society Interface|J R Soc Interface]] |volume=7 |issue=53 |pages=1735–1743 | doi=10.1098/rsif.2010.0111|pmc=2988264 |pmid=20462875 }}</ref>

[[File:Green Eggs and Ham word adjacency network.png|600px|thumb|Network of concatenated words from ''Green Eggs and Ham'', by [[Dr. Seuss]]. If word 1 appears immediately before word 2 in at least one sentence in the text, a directed edge (arrow) is placed from word 1 to word 2. The height of each word is proportional to its trophic level. Colours indicate syntactic function; from lowest to highest mean trophic level: nouns (blue), prepositions and conjunctions (cyan), determiners (pink), adverbs (yellow), pronouns (green), verbs (red), and adjectives (purple). When a word has more than one function, the one most common in the text is used.]]

The relation between trophic level and node function can be seen in networks other than food webs. The figure shows a word adjacency network derived from the book ''[[Green Eggs and Ham]]'', by Dr. Seuss.<ref name="johnson2017"/> The height of nodes represents their trophic levels (according here to the edge direction which is the opposite of that suggested by the arrows, which indicate the order in which words are concatenated in sentences). The syntactic function of words is also shown with node colour. There is a clear relationship between syntactic function and trophic level: the mean trophic level of common nouns (blue) is <math>s_{noun} = 1.4 \pm 1.2</math>, whereas that of verbs (red) is <math>s_{verb} = 7.0 \pm 2.7</math>.
This example illustrates how trophic coherence or incoherence might emerge from node function, and also that the trophic structure of networks provides a means of identifying node function in certain systems.

== Generating trophically coherent networks ==

There are various ways of generating directed networks with specified trophic coherence, all based on gradually introducing new edges 
to the system in such a way that the probability of each new candidate edge being accepted depends on the expected trophic difference it would have.
 
The ''preferential preying model'' is an evolving network model similar to the [[Barabási–Albert model|Barábasi-Albert model]] of [[preferential attachment]], but inspired on an ecosystem that grows through immigration of new species.<ref name="johnson2014"/>
One begins with <math>B</math> basal nodes and proceeds to introduce new nodes up to a total of <math>N</math>.
Each new node <math>i</math> is assigned a first in-neighbour <math>j</math> (a prey species in the food-web context) and a new 
edge is placed from <math>j</math> to <math>i</math>. The new node is given a temporary trophic level <math>s_i^t=s_j+1</math>.
Then a further <math>\kappa_i</math> new in-neighbours <math>l</math> are chosen for <math>i</math> from among those in the network according to their trophic levels. Specifically, for a new candidate in-neighbour <math>l</math>, the probability of being chosen is a function of 
<math>x_{il}^t=s_i^t-s_l</math>. Johnson ''et al''<ref name="johnson2014"/> use
::<math>
P_{il}\propto \exp\left(-\frac{|x_{il}^t-1|}{T}\right),
</math>
where <math>T</math> is a parameter which tunes the trophic coherence: for <math>T=0</math> maximally coherent networks are generated, and
<math>q</math> increases monotonically with <math>T</math> for <math>T>0</math>.
The choice of <math>\kappa_i</math> is arbitrary. One possibility is to 
set to <math>\kappa_i=z_i n_i</math>,
where <math>n_i</math> is the number of nodes already in the network when <math>i</math> arrives, and <math>z_i</math> is a random variable drawn from a [[Beta distribution]]
with parameters <math>\alpha=1</math> and
::<math>
\beta=\frac{N^2-B^2}{2L_d}-1
</math>
(<math>L_d</math> being the desired number of edges).
This way, the ''generalised cascade model''<ref name="cohen1985">{{cite journal |author=Cohen JE and Newman CM |year=1985 |title=A stochastic theory of community food webs I. Models and aggregated data |journal=[[Proc. R. Soc. B]] |volume=224 |issue=1237 |pages=421–448 |doi=10.1098/rspb.1985.0042|bibcode=1985RSPSB.224..421C |s2cid=52993453 }}</ref><ref name="stouffer2006">{{cite journal |author=Stouffer DB, Camacho J, Amaral LAN |year=2006 |title=A robust measure of food web intervality |journal=[[Proc Natl Acad Sci USA]] |volume=103 |issue=50 |pages=19015–19020|doi=10.1073/pnas.0603844103 |pmid=17146055 |pmc=1748169 |bibcode=2006PNAS..10319015S |doi-access=free }}</ref> is recovered in the limit <math>T\rightarrow \infty</math>, and the degree distributions are as in the ''niche model''<ref name="willilams2000">{{cite journal |author=Williams RJ and Martinez ND |year=2000 |title=Simple rules yield complex food webs |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=404 |issue=6774 |pages=180–183|doi=10.1038/35004572 |pmid=10724169 |bibcode=2000Natur.404..180W |s2cid=205004984 }}</ref> and ''generalised niche model''.<ref name="stouffer2006"/>
This algorithm, as described above, generates networks with no cycles (except for self-cycles, if the new node <math>i</math> is itself considered among its candidate in-neighbours <math>l</math>). In order for cycles of all lengths to be a possible, one can consider new candidate edges in which the new node <math>i</math> is the in-neighbour as well as those in which it would be the out-neighbour. The probability of acceptance of these edges, 
<math>P_{li}</math>, then depends on <math>x_{li}^t=s_l-s_i^t</math>.

The ''generalised preferential preying model''<ref name="klaise2016"/> is similar to the one described above, but has certain advantages. In particular, it is more analytically tractable, and one can generate networks with a precise number of edges <math>L</math>.
The network begins with <math>B</math> basal nodes, and then a further <math>N-B</math> new nodes are added in the following way. When each enters the system, it is assigned a single in-neighbour randomly from among those already there. Every node then has an integer temporary trophic level 
<math>s_i^t</math>. The remaining <math>L-N+B</math> edges are introduced as follows. Each pair of nodes <math>(i,j)</math> has two temporary trophic distances associated, <math>x_{ij}^t=s_i^t-s_j^t</math> and <math>x_{ji}^t=s_j^t-s_i^t</math>. Each of these candidate edges is accepted with a probability that depends on this temporary distance. Klaise and Johnson<ref name="klaise2016"/> use
::<math>
P_{ij}\propto \exp\left(-\frac{(x_{ij}^t-1)^2}{2T^2}\right),
</math>
because they find the distribution of trophic distances in several kinds of networks to be approximately [[Normal distribution|normal]], and this choice leads to a range of the parameter <math>T</math> in which <math>q \simeq T</math>. Once all the edges have been introduced, one must recalculate the trophic levels of all nodes, since these will differ from the temporary ones originally assigned unless <math>T \simeq 0</math>.
As with the preferential preying model, the average incoherence parameter <math>q</math> of the resulting networks is a monotonically increasing function of <math>T</math> for <math>T \geq 0</math>. The figure above shows two networks with different trophic coherence generated with this algorithm.
